cues.text: Let us close this study session with a set of independent revision questions, written by your tutor.
Treat them as a self-test.
Pause after each question, try to answer it in your own words, and then compare your answer with the one given.
There are seven questions, and we will take them in order.
Question one.
A clinic scans its existing paper cards but keeps the same manual approval process.
Is this transformation?
The answer is: this is digitisation, not full transformation.
The medium changed, but the operating model did not.
Let us unpack that.
Digitisation means converting information from an analogue form, such as a paper card, into a digital form, such as a scanned file.
That is exactly what the clinic did.
But look at what stayed the same: the approval process is still manual, so people still route, check and sign off in the same way as before.
Digital transformation, by contrast, changes how the organisation operates and creates value.
Here, only the medium moved from paper to digital file.
The way the clinic works, its operating model, is untouched.
So we call this digitisation, and we do not call it full transformation.
Question two.
A logistics firm redesigns its services around digital routing, booking and real-time customer visibility.
Which transformation layers are involved?
The answer lists seven layers: strategy, processes, technology, integration and data, infrastructure, people, and customer experience.
Notice how different this is from the clinic.
The logistics firm is not simply converting something to a digital format.
It is redesigning its services around digital capabilities.
Digital routing and booking change how work flows, so processes are involved.
The routing and booking systems are technology.
For them to work together, and for customers to see shipments in real time, the firm needs integration and data, and the infrastructure that supports it.
Because the services themselves are redesigned, strategy is involved.
The staff who dispatch, drive and support customers must work in new ways, so people are involved.
And real-time customer visibility is a direct change in customer experience.
A useful habit when you meet a scenario like this is to walk through all seven layers, one after another, and ask whether each is touched.
Question three.
What is the difference between innovation and invention?
The answer: innovation implements value-creating novelty, while invention is the creation of a new idea or device.
So an invention is about coming up with something new.
An innovation is about putting novelty into use so that it creates value.
A brilliant new device sitting in a laboratory is an invention.
It becomes an innovation only when it is implemented in a way that creates value.
The key word in the definition of innovation is implementation.
Question four.
A firm buys a costly cloud platform without defining objectives.
What is the major strategic risk?
The answer: misalignment, wasted investment, and no measurable benefits.
Think about why.
Without defined objectives, nobody can say what the platform is supposed to achieve.
The purchase is therefore not aligned with the firm's strategy, which is the first risk, misalignment.
The money spent may deliver little, which is wasted investment.
And because there was no objective to measure against, the firm cannot show any measurable benefits.
Technology should follow strategy, and not the other way round.
Question five.
Why might a monolith remain appropriate for a small service?
The answer: a monolith offers simpler deployment, debugging and transactions, and microservices are not mandatory for agility.
A monolith is an application built and deployed as a single unit.
For a small service, that brings three practical advantages named in the answer.
Deployment is simpler, because there is one unit to release.
Debugging is simpler, because you are tracing problems within one application.
And transactions are simpler, because the operations happen together rather than being spread across many separate services.
The important lesson is that microservices, which split an application into many small independent services, are not mandatory in order to be agile.
The right architecture depends on the situation.
Question six.
Which metric most directly demonstrates a successful digital payment workflow: the number of servers, or the successful transaction rate?
The answer: the transaction success rate, because it reflects the customer and business outcome.
The number of servers describes how much infrastructure you have, but it does not tell you whether customers are actually paying successfully.
The transaction success rate tells you exactly that.
It shows whether the workflow delivers the result that customers and the business care about.
A good key performance indicator, or KPI, measures outcomes, not just the technical resources behind them.
Question seven.
Explain why culture matters even when technology works.
The answer: employees must understand, adopt and improve new processes, and technical deployment alone does not create benefits.
Consider what that means.
A system can be installed and function perfectly from a technical point of view.
But if staff do not understand it, do not use it, or do not improve how it is used, the organisation will not gain the benefits.
Benefits come from people working in new ways.
That is why culture matters: it determines whether employees understand, adopt and continually improve the new processes.
Technical deployment is necessary, but on its own it does not create benefits.
That completes the seven revision questions.
Try them again later without looking at the answers, and see whether you can reproduce each reason, not just each conclusion.
